title: Heat capacity as a marker for shape and jamming transitions in active systems
abstract: Persistence influences the stationary states of active particles, producing boundary accumulation at the single-particle level, and clustering or jamming in interacting systems. These features disappear as the persistence decreases and the system approaches a more passive-like stationary state. We show that these transitions have a distinct calorimetric signature. Using a lattice run-and-tumble dynamics, consistent with local detailed balance, we compute the nonequilibrium heat capacity from the excess heat released following a small temperature perturbation. For a single particle confined between reflecting boundaries, the heat capacity develops a maximum in the persistence regime corresponding to shape transition. Adding an exclusion interaction to the active particles on a periodic lattice, the reorganization of jammed clusters produces a corresponding peak in the thermal response. We also discuss the impact of the time-symmetric part of the transition rates, and show the possibility of seeing the same signatures of heat response in experiments by AC calorimetry. Our results show that nonequilibrium heat capacities can serve as calorimetric probes of nonequilibrium phase transitions.
summary: This work demonstrates that the nonequilibrium heat capacity can act as a sensitive thermodynamic probe for structural phase transitions in active matter. By modeling single and interacting active particles, the authors show that sharp peaks in the heat capacity signal the onset or reorganization of jammed or shape-transitional states. This suggests a powerful experimental avenue for characterizing non-equilibrium phase transitions.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether nonequilibrium heat capacity can serve as a measurable thermodynamic signature for structural phase transitions, such as shape or jamming, occurring in active matter systems driven far from equilibrium.
main_result: The nonequilibrium heat capacity exhibits distinct, non-monotonic peaks corresponding to the structural transitions, confirming its potential as a calorimetric probe for these active matter phase changes.
method: The authors calculate the excess heat and nonequilibrium heat capacity by analyzing the relaxation dynamics of the system's probability distribution following a small temperature perturbation.
model_or_system: The models include single active particles confined between boundaries and interacting run-and-tumble (RTP) particles on a periodic lattice, whose dynamics are governed by Markov jump processes.
key_observables: Nonequilibrium heat capacity ($C$), stationary density profiles ($ho_i$), and mean block size ($\ell$).
important_parameters: Persistence rate ($\alpha$), system size ($L$), and temperature perturbation ($\Delta T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on calculating the *excess* heat and assumes local detailed balance for the spatial hopping rates in the lattice model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structural crossover (e.g., mean block size vs. persistence rate) alongside the corresponding non-monotonic heat capacity response for both single and interacting particle systems.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework for calculating nonequilibrium heat capacity. It then applies this to the single-particle case (boundary effects) and extends the analysis to interacting particles (jamming transitions), concluding with numerical methods for AC calorimetry.
why_interesting: The connection drawn between non-equilibrium thermodynamics (heat capacity) and non-equilibrium phase transitions (active matter) provides a novel, measurable diagnostic tool applicable to complex, non-equilibrium many-body systems.
